speaker: Casey Handmer
title: Why Elon Outcompetes Everyone | Casey Handmer, Terraform Industries
question: In orbital infrastructure, why does space-based solar power fail economically compared to beaming modulated data or AI compute from orbit?
guest: Space-based solar power is kind of dumb, because you're taking a product where it's expensive and selling it somewhere where it's cheap, which is not what a business should do. In space, power is really expensive, and then you're beaming that power as undifferentiated microwaves down to Earth where you have to compete with solar, nuclear, coal, and gas for maybe ten cents a kilowatt-hour. However, Starlink works because instead of just beaming microwaves at Earth for power, they modulate those microwaves with a radio signal that transmits not power, but information. If you run the math on revenue per watt of transmitted microwave power for Starlink, it's a billion times higher than space-based solar power. Then you put compute satellites in sun-synchronous orbit so they're always in the sun except during eclipses, so you don't need anywhere near as many batteries, and you use laser links to transmit data. Instead of transmitting Netflix—where the marginal bit isn't worth much—you transmit tokens of a hyper-intelligent model. The comparative value of an AI token bit versus an average broadband bit is probably at least 1,000 times more valuable.

points.core: Space-based solar generates power expensively in orbit to sell cheaply on Earth.
points.note: Accept: producing undifferentiated electricity in a high-cost orbital environment to compete against cheap terrestrial merchant power (~$0.05-$0.10/kWh) violates basic arbitrage. Do not credit: generic claims that beaming power is technically hard or dangerous.

points.core: Modulating orbital microwaves for data yields roughly billionfold higher revenue per watt.
points.note: Accept: encoding information onto the radio or microwave signal (like satellite broadband) earns orders of magnitude (millions to billions of times) more revenue per watt than raw power transmission. Do not credit: generic statements that communications satellites are profitable.

points.core: Transmitting AI tokens multiplies economic value per bit dramatically over streaming video.
points.note: Accept: AI inference tokens command orders of magnitude (~100x-1,000x+) higher economic value per transmitted bit than commodity consumer bandwidth like streaming video. Do not credit: vague hype about AI demand without comparing value per bit or bandwidth.

points.core: Sun-synchronous orbits keep compute satellites continuously illuminated to avoid heavy battery mass.
points.note: Accept: dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbits provide near-constant sunlight (aside from brief eclipses), drastically cutting onboard battery mass requirements. Do not credit: generic statements that there is lots of sunlight in space.

models.answer:
Space-based solar power struggles because it sells a cheap commodity delivered through a lossy, capital-heavy chain, while data and compute sell high-value products that are easy to transmit. Note that the premise is only partly settled: orbital AI compute is itself unproven economically.

Electricity is worth only a few cents per kilowatt-hour on the ground, where terrestrial solar plus batteries keeps getting cheaper. To compete, an orbital power station must convert sunlight to electricity, then to microwaves or lasers, beam it roughly 36,000 km from geostationary orbit, and reconvert it, losing most of the energy end to end. Diffraction forces kilometre-scale transmit antennas and multi-kilometre ground rectennas, so launch mass, assembly and maintenance costs are enormous for a low-margin output.

Data flips the equation. A communications satellite's value lies in the information modulated onto the beam, not the energy, so watts of signal earn revenue that would take megawatts of delivered power to match. Orbital compute similarly uses the solar power in place and downlinks only results, avoiding the power-beaming losses, though it faces its own hurdles in heat rejection, radiation, launch cost and servicing.

The response omits the link between near-continuous illumination in sun-synchronous orbit and reduced battery mass.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Space-based solar power fails economically because it uses expensive orbital mass to deliver a cheap commodity, bulk electricity worth mere cents per kilowatt-hour, across a punishingly lossy transmission chain. Beaming power to Earth requires converting direct current into microwaves or lasers, traversing the atmosphere, and rectifying it back into grid electricity. Wave diffraction demands kilometer-scale orbital apertures and vast ground rectennas, while compounding conversion and atmospheric losses waste over half the captured energy, leaving orbital hardware unable to compete with cheap terrestrial generation.

Conversely, orbital AI compute and communications consume continuous solar power locally as direct current and beam down modulated bits instead of raw joules. Because information value scales with bandwidth rather than delivered energy, a compact, low-power laser or radio link can transmit gigabits per second of high-margin AI tokens or data to small ground terminals. Moving silicon to the sunlight eliminates massive power-beaming arrays, rectennas, and terrestrial grid bottlenecks, generating orders of magnitude more revenue per launched kilogram and per captured photon.

points.why: The response directly ties high orbital costs to the low price of competing terrestrial electricity.
quotes: it uses expensive orbital mass to deliver a cheap commodity, bulk electricity worth mere cents per kilowatt-hour
leaving orbital hardware unable to compete with cheap terrestrial generation

points.why: The response describes signal modulation and claims higher revenue per launched kilogram and captured photon, leaving the required million- to billionfold revenue advantage per transmitted watt unstated.
Calling AI tokens high-margin does not establish that their value per transmitted bit is orders of magnitude greater than that of streaming video or other commodity broadband.
The response mentions continuous solar power without linking near-continuous illumination to a sun-synchronous orbit and reduced battery mass.

A few watts of laser or radio downlink can carry terabits of low-latency traffic or valuable AI tokens, generating orders of magnitude more revenue per watt and per kilogram launched. Converting photons into bits in orbit eliminates massive power-beaming infrastructure while trading low-margin kilowatt-hours for premium digital services.

The main reason is that electricity is a cheap, low-value commodity, while information is worth far more per joule.

Space-based solar power has to deliver the energy itself. Diffraction means a beam from GEO needs transmitter and rectenna apertures kilometres across. Converting DC to microwaves, sending them through the atmosphere and converting back to DC loses roughly half to most of the energy. All that hardware must then compete with ground solar plus batteries at a few cents per kilowatt-hour. Launch, assembly and maintenance costs swamp revenue that is capped at wholesale power prices.

A data link is different. It only needs to carry enough signal for the receiver to decode bits above the noise, so watts of transmitted power can deliver gigabits worth far more than the energy used. Orbital compute goes further: it uses the sunlight on the spot to run chips, so no power is beamed down at all. Only the results come down, such as model outputs or processed imagery, and those carry the highest value per joule.

So orbit makes economic sense when you turn sunlight into bits in space and send down the bits, not the energy. Orbital datacentres still have real problems, especially getting rid of heat, radiation damage and launch cost.

Space-based solar power fails economically because it tries to sell a low-margin commodity—raw electricity—while paying the steep capital and launch costs of orbital infrastructure. Beaming bulk power to Earth suffers from compounding conversion losses across solar cells, microwave or laser transmitters, and ground receivers, and physics dictates kilometer-scale orbital arrays and massive terrestrial rectennas to manage diffraction and keep beam intensities safe. Even with cheap launches, the resulting electricity struggles to compete with rapidly falling terrestrial solar and battery storage costs.

By contrast, using orbital solar power to run AI compute or beam modulated data monetizes high-value information rather than raw watts. Each watt used for computation or communications generates orders of magnitude more revenue per kilogram launched than selling electricity to the grid. Because information requires far less transmit power than bulk energy, orbital data and compute systems can use compact laser or RF terminals and small ground stations, sidestepping the colossal hardware, land-use, and efficiency penalties that make orbital power beaming uncompetitive.

Space-based solar power has to deliver enough physical energy to sell electricity at a competitive price per kilowatt-hour. A viable system would need to launch and maintain large solar arrays and transmitters, spread the beam over a ground receiver, and absorb losses as electricity is converted into a beam and back again. More orbital sunlight helps, but the delivered power still has to compete with cheap terrestrial generation.

A data link only needs enough received energy for the receiver to distinguish the bits reliably. If an orbital computer processes satellite imagery and sends down a small set of detections, the customer pays for the result, and the downlink carries only a fraction of the raw data. That can make sense when the data already originates in space. For ordinary AI workloads, launch costs, heat rejection, hardware replacement, and connectivity still make Earth-based data centers hard to beat.

Space-based solar power has to sell kilowatt-hours. To deliver a gigawatt on Earth, an orbital system must collect more than a gigawatt of sunlight, convert it to a beam, and convert the beam back to electricity. Those losses increase the collector area and hardware that must be launched and maintained. The delivered electricity still has to compete with terrestrial power prices.

A data link earns revenue from the information encoded in the beam. The receiver only needs enough signal to decode the bits, so a modest amount of transmitted energy can deliver a valuable result. Orbital AI can exploit that difference when the data already originates in space. A satellite might analyze a large image and transmit a small, time-sensitive wildfire alert. The customer pays for the warning, and the operator saves downlink capacity. General-purpose AI compute in orbit has a weaker case because launch, cooling, and communications costs still have to beat the economics of a terrestrial data center.
